A prominent rock formation leans away and juts outward over the cliff line to the right of the waterfall, tempting visiting rock climbers. Sunshine illuminates the rocks’ varied minerals make a colorful patchwork of grays, oranges, creams and browns along the cliff face.", "heading_path": "OVERVIEW: Front Side of Brochure > IMAGE and TEXT: Granite Cliffs", "kind": "paragraph", "start": 17001, "end": 17594}, {"text": "CAPTION: Granite Cliffs", "heading_path": "OVERVIEW: Front Side of Brochure > IMAGE and TEXT: Granite Cliffs", "kind": "paragraph", "start": 17596, "end": 17619}, {"text": "CREDIT: Laurence Parent", "heading_path": "OVERVIEW: Front Side of Brochure > IMAGE and TEXT: Granite Cliffs", "kind": "paragraph", "start": 17621, "end": 17644}, {"text": "RELATED TEXT: The massive cliffs of Yosemite and Hetch Hetchy valleys challenge the body and mind, especially the inquisitive nature of human beings. When an 1868 Yosemite guidebook declared, “the summit of Half Dome will never be trodden by human foot,” it was taken as a challenge. George Anderson reached the top in 1875. Countless others followed. One by one, adventurous men and women made other first ascents on sheer granite walls in Yosemite, changing the sport of climbing forever. The challenge of these cliffs continues to beckon climbers from around the world.", "heading_path": "OVERVIEW: Front Side of Brochure > IMAGE and TEXT: Granite Cliffs", "kind": "paragraph", "start": 17646, "end": 18218}, {"text": "The very existence of great cliffs like Half Dome and El Capitan has inspired questions about how they came to be. American Indians tell of a woman and her husband who argued and fought. The displeased spirits changed them into stone, Half Dome and North Dome, forever to face each other across the Valley. How these cliffs were formed has challenged geologists for over 100 years. They think the granite of Yosemite’s walls solidified over five miles underground. As the overlying rock eroded away, the granites rose to their current exposed level. Nature’s dynamic forces continue sculpting this exposed rock.", "heading_path": "OVERVIEW: Front Side of Brochure > IMAGE and TEXT: Granite Cliffs", "kind": "paragraph", "start": 18220, "end": 18831}, {"text": "IMAGE: On the Salathe Wall of El Capitan", "heading_path": "OVERVIEW: Front Side of Brochure > IMAGE: On the Salathe Wall of El Capitan", "kind": "paragraph", "start": 18833, "end": 18873}, {"text": "DESCRIBING: A small black and white photo", "heading_path": "OVERVIEW: Front Side of Brochure > IMAGE: On the Salathe Wall of El Capitan", "kind": "paragraph", "start": 18875, "end": 18916}, {"text": "SYNOPSIS: A small black and white, circular photo from 1961 is captioned \"On the Salathe Wall of El Capitan.” It features a young adult, male climber, Tom Frost. He is wearing a white shirt with sleeves rolled up to his biceps and hanging by a climbing rope on a rock wall. His climbing harness and the taut rope attached to it allow him to rest in a semi-seated pose. His left hand rests casually on the cluttered climbing rack of gear that dangle from his waist while his right hand steadies himself on the rock. His broad muscular upper body is turned halfway back, toward the viewer. He is gazing back over his left shoulder, with a grin, as he gets a unique view of the vast landscape around and below him. His right knee is bent, pants rolled up below the knee and his ankle comfortably hanging in a loop of climbing gear. The flexed muscles are well defined on his left leg which is also bent. He appears to be bracing his foot on the rock, just out of the frame. He wears tan shoes which pre-date the sticky rubber-covered climbing shoes of today. Incongruously, the shoes look like he might be wearing them along a city street. The forested mountains, far below in the background, are topped with puffy clouds just over the ridge line.", "heading_path": "OVERVIEW: Front Side of Brochure > IMAGE: On the Salathe Wall of El Capitan", "kind": "paragraph", "start": 18918, "end": 20162}, {"text": "CAPTION: On the Salathe Wall of El Capitan", "heading_path": "OVERVIEW: Front Side of Brochure > IMAGE: On the Salathe Wall of El Capitan", "kind": "paragraph", "start": 20164, "end": 20206}, {"text": "CREDIT: Copyright © TOM FROST COLLECTION COURTESY YOSEMITE CLIMBING ASSOCIATION", "heading_path": "OVERVIEW: Front Side of Brochure > IMAGE: On the Salathe Wall of El Capitan", "kind": "paragraph", "start": 20208, "end": 20287}, {"text": "IMAGE: Peregrine Falcon", "heading_path": "OVERVIEW: Front Side of Brochure > IMAGE: Peregrine Falcon", "kind": "paragraph", "start": 20289, "end": 20312}, {"text": "DESCRIBING: Vignette image of a peregrine falcon.", "heading_path": "OVERVIEW: Front Side of Brochure > IMAGE: Peregrine Falcon", "kind": "paragraph", "start": 20314, "end": 20363}, {"text": "SYNOPSIS: The cutout photo shows a clear view of a peregrine falcon, ( Falco peregrinus ) soaring in flight, wings stretched out wide and lifted slightly above its body. Its wingspan is somewhere between 2.5 and 4 feet (roughly one meter). The detail of the gray-brown tops of its wings and finely barred black and white underwings are clear. The falcon's black-tipped yellow beak is slightly open and its steel-gray head and \"sideburns\" contrast starkly against its white neck and \"cheeks.\" Its body is covered in vertical black and white barring and its orange-colored legs and feet are curled back for aerodynamics.", "heading_path": "OVERVIEW: Front Side of Brochure > IMAGE: Peregrine Falcon", "kind": "paragraph", "start": 20365, "end": 20983}, {"text": "CAPTION: Peregrine Falcon", "heading_path": "OVERVIEW: Front Side of Brochure > IMAGE: Peregrine Falcon", "kind": "paragraph", "start": 20985, "end": 21010}, {"text": "CREDIT: NPS / James McGrew", "heading_path": "OVERVIEW: Front Side of Brochure > IMAGE: Peregrine Falcon", "kind": "paragraph", "start": 21012, "end": 21038}, {"text": "IMAGE: Rockfall", "heading_path": "OVERVIEW: Front Side of Brochure > IMAGE: Rockfall", "kind": "paragraph", "start": 21040, "end": 21055}, {"text": "DESCRIBING: Photo of a large waterfall flowing over granite cliff walls.", "heading_path": "OVERVIEW: Front Side of Brochure > IMAGE: Rockfall", "kind": "paragraph", "start": 21057, "end": 21129}, {"text": "SYNOPSIS: This photo showcases a white cascading waterfall plummeting down from a grey-toned granite rock wall. The waterfall is full and looks as if a mighty wind is blowing its waters to the left, making the waterfall look dramatic and powerful. In the middle of the rock wall located to the right of the waterfall is a large, blackened area. Text reads, \"Dark streaks are caused by lichens.\" Centered in the black area is a noticeably light-colored patch of rock. Accompanying text indicates, \"Light scar reveals a fresh rockfall.\"", "heading_path": "OVERVIEW: Front Side of Brochure > IMAGE: Rockfall", "kind": "paragraph", "start": 21131, "end": 21665}, {"text": "CAPTION: Rockfall continually changes Yosemite’s great cliffs at a rate difficult to chart in the comparative brevity of human lifetimes. Water, ice, plants, and gravity have worked on these granite walls for millions of years and continue to shape them today.", "heading_path": "OVERVIEW: Front Side of Brochure > IMAGE: Rockfall", "kind": "paragraph", "start": 21667, "end": 21927}, {"text": "CREDIT: Copyright Fred Hirschmann", "heading_path": "OVERVIEW: Front Side of Brochure > IMAGE: Rockfall", "kind": "paragraph", "start": 21929, "end": 21962}, {"text": "IMAGE: Seqouia Cones", "heading_path": "OVERVIEW: Front Side of Brochure > IMAGE: Seqouia Cones", "kind": "paragraph", "start": 21964, "end": 21984}, {"text": "DESCRIBING: An oval picture faded around the edges showing five sequoia cones.", "heading_path": "OVERVIEW: Front Side of Brochure > IMAGE: Seqouia Cones", "kind": "paragraph", "start": 21986, "end": 22064}, {"text": "SYNOPSIS: The image shows five light brown sequoia cones, resembles a pinecone, that are bunched together. Four of the sequoia cones are lying sideways while one is upright. They are the egg-shaped and vary in length between 2-3 inches and 5-8 cm, with cross hatching indentations that create horizontal diamond shapes around the cone with a little dimple in the middle of each diamond, vaguely resembling a pair of pursed lips. The diamond shaped segments are tightly packed together, like shingles on a roof, giving the cones a dense, sturdy appearance. The surface of the cones is textured but smooth, like hardened ripples. The image is faded around the edges in an oval shape, but long, light brown pine needs are seen cushioning the pile of sequoia cones, suggesting the cones’ location on the forest floor.", "heading_path": "OVERVIEW: Front Side of Brochure > IMAGE: Seqouia Cones", "kind": "paragraph", "start": 22066, "end": 22879}, {"text": "CAPTION: Sequoia cones", "heading_path": "OVERVIEW: Front Side of Brochure > IMAGE: Seqouia Cones", "kind": "paragraph", "start": 22881, "end": 22903}, {"text": "CREDIT: Copyright John Elk III", "heading_path": "OVERVIEW: Front Side of Brochure > IMAGE: Seqouia Cones", "kind": "paragraph", "start": 22905, "end": 22935}, {"text": "IMAGE: Chickaree", "heading_path": "OVERVIEW: Front Side of Brochure > IMAGE: Chickaree", "kind": "paragraph", "start": 22937, "end": 22953}, {"text": "DESCRIBING: A small, cutout color picture showing a Chickaree squirrel clinging to a tree.", "heading_path": "OVERVIEW: Front Side of Brochure > IMAGE: Chickaree", "kind": "paragraph", "start": 22955, "end": 23045}, {"text": "SYNOPSIS: The cutout image, captioned \"Chickaree,\" shows the front half of a bi-colored chickaree squirrel, ( Tamiasciurus douglasii ) peeking out to the right, from behind a grey roughly-textured tree trunk. The upper half of the head, neck, and body is a rusty brown with bits of black on the forehead, cheeks and nose, while the squirrel’s underside and belly is grey. The little-clawed paws of its two front limbs are grasping the tree, while the body and head stretch forward, nose pointing out as if it smells something. Its large walnut-shaped eyes are open wide and surrounded by a ring of white. Its small, round ears are alert and perked to either side, with tufts of rusty brown fur rimming their edges.", "heading_path": "OVERVIEW: Front Side of Brochure > IMAGE: Chickaree", "kind": "paragraph", "start": 23047, "end": 23761}, {"text": "CAPTION: Chickaree", "heading_path": "OVERVIEW: Front Side of Brochure > IMAGE: Chickaree", "kind": "paragraph", "start": 23763, "end": 23781}, {"text": "CREDIT: Copyright Roberta Stacy", "heading_path": "OVERVIEW: Front Side of Brochure > IMAGE: Chickaree", "kind": "paragraph", "start": 23783, "end": 23814}, {"text": "IMAGE and TEXT: Pacific Dogwood", "heading_path": "OVERVIEW: Front Side of Brochure > IMAGE and TEXT: Pacific Dogwood", "kind": "paragraph", "start": 23816, "end": 23847}, {"text": "DESCRIBING: A floating image of Pacific dogwood flowers over the black background of the brochure.", "heading_path": "OVERVIEW: Front Side of Brochure > IMAGE and TEXT: Pacific Dogwood", "kind": "paragraph", "start": 23849, "end": 23947}, {"text": "SYNOPSIS: Six white dogwood \"flowers,\" ( Cornus nuttallii ) seem to hover in space against the black background of the brochure, rather than covering a dogwood tree, as they usually do. The large and solitary white flowers are imposters, actually a clump of tiny greenish-yellow flowers surrounded by 4 to 8 creamy white leaves called bracts. The bracts look just like large white petals, each one curling and bowing uniquely. Every \"flower\" has the tips of green leaves peeking from beneath the white bracts.", "heading_path": "OVERVIEW: Front Side of Brochure > IMAGE and TEXT: Pacific Dogwood", "kind": "paragraph", "start": 23949, "end": 24458}, {"text": "CAPTION: Pacific dogwood", "heading_path": "OVERVIEW: Front Side of Brochure > IMAGE and TEXT: Pacific Dogwood", "kind": "paragraph", "start": 24460, "end": 24484}, {"text": "CREDIT: Copyright John Elk III", "heading_path": "OVERVIEW: Front Side of Brochure > IMAGE and TEXT: Pacific Dogwood", "kind": "paragraph", "start": 24486, "end": 24516}, {"text": "RELATED TEXT: Changes brought about by fire don’t benefit just the sequoia. Pacific dogwoods need the filtered sunlight that can reach into a sequoia grove if periodic fire keeps its understory open.", "heading_path": "OVERVIEW: Front Side of Brochure > IMAGE and TEXT: Pacific Dogwood", "kind": "paragraph", "start": 24518, "end": 24717}, {"text": "IMAGE and TEXT: The Snow Plant", "heading_path": "OVERVIEW: Front Side of Brochure > IMAGE and TEXT: The Snow Plant", "kind": "paragraph", "start": 24719, "end": 24749}, {"text": "DESCRIBING: A small color cutout photograph of three snow plants.", "heading_path": "OVERVIEW: Front Side of Brochure > IMAGE and TEXT: The Snow Plant", "kind": "paragraph", "start": 24751, "end": 24816}, {"text": "SYNOPSIS: Three alien-looking plants burst through the forest floor in a tight clump in this small cutout photograph. Every part of the plant (the stalks, leaves, and petals) is a uniform color of striking candy-apple red! About a foot tall, with meaty red stalks, the texture of their fleshy bodies looks like they might be related to mushrooms, although they aren't. At a glance, the plants' shape resembles a collection of upright, scarlet-colored pinecones balanced atop short and thick stems. Rather than woody scales, the stalks are densely covered with diagonal rows of fleshy crimson leaves. These leaves look more like curling elongated Halloween fingernails than any familiar leaf shape. Tucked uniformly between each red leaf are ruby colored flowers, their petals fused to make outward facing bells. A small portion of the forest floor where the red snow plants protrude from is visible, covered in pine needs and sequoia cones.", "heading_path": "OVERVIEW: Front Side of Brochure > IMAGE and TEXT: The Snow Plant", "kind": "paragraph", "start": 24818, "end": 25758}, {"text": "CAPTION: The snow plant", "heading_path": "OVERVIEW: Front Side of Brochure > IMAGE and TEXT: The Snow Plant", "kind": "paragraph", "start": 25760, "end": 25783}, {"text": "CREDIT: Larry Ulrich", "heading_path": "OVERVIEW: Front Side of Brochure > IMAGE and TEXT: The Snow Plant", "kind": "paragraph", "start": 25785, "end": 25805}, {"text": "RELATED TEXT: The snow plant (left) gets water and nutrients from fungi, which are connected to tree roots.", "heading_path": "OVERVIEW: Front Side of Brochure > IMAGE and TEXT: The Snow Plant", "kind": "paragraph", "start": 25807, "end": 25914}, {"text": "IMAGE: Sequoia Fires", "heading_path": "OVERVIEW: Front Side of Brochure > IMAGE: Sequoia Fires", "kind": "paragraph", "start": 25916, "end": 25936}, {"text": "DESCRIBING: A small color photograph of a sequoia grove on fire.", "heading_path": "OVERVIEW: Front Side of Brochure > IMAGE: Sequoia Fires", "kind": "paragraph", "start": 25938, "end": 26002}, {"text": "SYNOPSIS: The image captures the bright glow of a fire on a forest floor at night. Two large black tree trunks in the foreground, one on either side of the image, frame the bright flames consuming the forest floor. A group of about six tall and slender trees and a small shrub, stand in the midst of the blaze while a fallen log lays horizontally across the bottom of the photo. The fire is a concentrated white color on the forest floor that transitions upward into yellow, orange, and red hues that contrast with the blackness of night. Orange embers freckle the bottom of the black fallen log and the tree trunks in the foreground.", "heading_path": "OVERVIEW: Front Side of Brochure > IMAGE: Sequoia Fires", "kind": "paragraph", "start": 26004, "end": 26638}, {"text": "CAPTION: Giant sequoias need fire so they can reproduce.", "heading_path": "OVERVIEW: Front Side of Brochure > IMAGE: Sequoia Fires", "kind": "paragraph", "start": 26640, "end": 26696}, {"text": "CREDIT: RAYMOND GEHMAN / NATIONAL GEOGRAPHIC IMAGE COLLECTION", "heading_path": "OVERVIEW: Front Side of Brochure > IMAGE: Sequoia Fires", "kind": "paragraph", "start": 26698, "end": 26759}, {"text": "IMAGE and TEXT: Sequoia Groves", "heading_path": "OVERVIEW: Front Side of Brochure > IMAGE and TEXT: Sequoia Groves", "kind": "paragraph", "start": 26761, "end": 26791}, {"text": "DESCRIBING: A large circular photograph of a sequoia grove.", "heading_path": "OVERVIEW: Front Side of Brochure > IMAGE and TEXT: Sequoia Groves", "kind": "paragraph", "start": 26793, "end": 26852}, {"text": "SYNOPSIS: In the center, a large round color photo depicts an intimate look into a grove of giant sequoias ( Sequoiadendron giganteum ) with three of the furrowed, reddish-brown trunks visible in the circular photo. Because of their massive size, only a tiny portion of the trunks of the gigantic trees are visible in the shot. A small section of a gigantic sequoia trunk fills the right half of the frame, seeming so close that the viewer could reach out and touch it. Its huge scale, hefty solidity, and broad base is reminiscent of the leg of an elephant. The reddish-brown trunk is covered in a fibrous, vertically furrowed bark so deep that the inner furrows are darkly shaded. To the left, two more sequoia trees stand tall and straight, their bases widening toward the ground. The tree in front has a long narrow burn scar rising as a large slit from the Earth, wide enough for a person to duck a bit and squeeze into the presumed cavern inside. Powerfully fire resistant, despite the burn, the tree has healed the scar by growing bark around the edges of the hole. Between the trees, varied shades of green plants and shrubs fill the forest floor and the darker green of pine trees can be glimpsed in the background.", "heading_path": "OVERVIEW: Front Side of Brochure > IMAGE and TEXT: Sequoia Groves", "kind": "paragraph", "start": 26854, "end": 28078}, {"text": "CAPTION: SEQUOIA GROVES", "heading_path": "OVERVIEW: Front Side of Brochure > IMAGE and TEXT: Sequoia Groves", "kind": "paragraph", "start": 28080, "end": 28103}, {"text": "CREDIT: Copyright Larry Ulrich", "heading_path": "OVERVIEW: Front Side of Brochure > IMAGE and TEXT: Sequoia Groves", "kind": "paragraph", "start": 28105, "end": 28135}, {"text": "RELATED TEXT: SEQUOIA GROVES Giant sequoias dwarf even the largest pine and fir trees that live among them. Descendants of an ancient line of trees, they can live for over 2,000 years. Their trunks can reach over 25 feet thick! As symbols of longevity and strength, the giant sequoias played a major role in the creation of what is now Yosemite National Park. Throughout the National Park System, thousands of rangers wear uniform belts and hatbands embossed with images of the cones and foliage of these trees.", "heading_path": "OVERVIEW: Front Side of Brochure > IMAGE and TEXT: Sequoia Groves", "kind": "paragraph", "start": 28137, "end": 28648}, {"text": "President Lincoln signed the bill that set aside the Mariposa Grove, along with scenic Yosemite Valley, in 1864. After a fire started in the grove, we began a 100-year history of protecting these beloved trees from fire. While our intentions were good, we contributed to the loss of what we cared about so much. Through experimentation and research, we discovered that fire promotes reproduction of these giant trees. It clears away the competing firs and cedars and exposes bare mineral soil for the tiny seed to take root.", "heading_path": "OVERVIEW: Front Side of Brochure > IMAGE and TEXT: Sequoia Groves", "kind": "paragraph", "start": 28650, "end": 29174}, {"text": "IMAGE: Galen Clark", "heading_path": "OVERVIEW: Front Side of Brochure > IMAGE: Galen Clark", "kind": "paragraph", "start": 29176, "end": 29194}, {"text": "DESCRIBING: A small, historic black and white vertical photograph of Galen Clark.", "heading_path": "OVERVIEW: Front Side of Brochure > IMAGE: Galen Clark", "kind": "paragraph", "start": 29196, "end": 29277}, {"text": "SYNOPSIS: A small elongated oval daguerreotype depicts an aged and rugged Galen Clark, standing with his right hand holding the long barrel of a rifle that is resting on the ground.", "heading_path": "OVERVIEW: Front Side of Brochure > IMAGE: Galen Clark", "kind": "paragraph", "start": 29279, "end": 29460}, {"text": "IN-DEPTH DESCRIPTION: Galen Clark is wearing a checkered, collared, button-down shirt that peaks out from underneath a buttoned sweater, topped with a weather-beaten knee-length heavy coat. He has noticeably baggy worn pants that bunch up at the ankles. A fur and leather cross-body satchel is draped over his left shoulder and rests at his right hip. A few unidentifiable trinkets dangle off the satchel like key chains.", "heading_path": "OVERVIEW: Front Side of Brochure > IMAGE: Galen Clark", "kind": "paragraph", "start": 29462, "end": 29883}, {"text": "Clark has near shoulder-length, unkempt hair, and a scruffy beard and mustache that almost covers his mouth. His leathery, aged, expressionless face has deep-set eyes that are gazing into the distance to the left of the photographer. He is standing with his right hand holding onto a long rifle as if it were a walking stick, with the barrel facing up and the stock on the ground. His left hand looks dirt-covered and is resting at his side.", "heading_path": "OVERVIEW: Front Side of Brochure > IMAGE: Galen Clark", "kind": "paragraph", "start": 29885, "end": 30326}, {"text": "CAPTION: Galen Clark, Yosemite’s first official guardian", "heading_path": "OVERVIEW: Front Side of Brochure > IMAGE: Galen Clark", "kind": "paragraph", "start": 30328, "end": 30384}, {"text": "CREDIT: NPS / CARLETON E. WATKINS", "heading_path": "OVERVIEW: Front Side of Brochure > IMAGE: Galen Clark", "kind": "paragraph", "start": 30386, "end": 30419}, {"text": "IMAGE and TEXT: Valley Life", "heading_path": "OVERVIEW: Front Side of Brochure > IMAGE and TEXT: Valley Life", "kind": "paragraph", "start": 30421, "end": 30448}, {"text": "DESCRIBING: A circular image of a section of the Merced River in Autumn.", "heading_path": "OVERVIEW: Front Side of Brochure > IMAGE and TEXT: Valley Life", "kind": "paragraph", "start": 30450, "end": 30522}, {"text": "SYNOPSIS: In the center, a large circular photo titled \"Valley\" and credited to Joseph Holmes is of the Merced River depicted in low light with smooth slow-moving water. Along the banks are trees and grasses with the fall hues of brown, orange and gold. The dried grasses of the far bank are reflected in the still water. Beyond the waterside meadow, a grouping of tall pines stands against the base of a sheer granite cliff.", "heading_path": "OVERVIEW: Front Side of Brochure > IMAGE and TEXT: Valley Life", "kind": "paragraph", "start": 30524, "end": 30949}, {"text": "CAPTION: VALLEY When you see the relatively lazy summer Merced River, it can be difficult to imagine how the same river, even in flood stage, could bring such", "heading_path": "OVERVIEW: Front Side of Brochure > IMAGE and TEXT: Valley Life", "kind": "paragraph", "start": 30951, "end": 31109}, {"text": "dramatic change throughout the Valley—rearranging boulders, roads, and campgrounds.", "heading_path": "OVERVIEW: Front Side of Brochure > IMAGE and TEXT: Valley Life", "kind": "paragraph", "start": 31111, "end": 31194}, {"text": "CREDIT: Copyright Joseph Holmes", "heading_path": "OVERVIEW: Front Side of Brochure > IMAGE and TEXT: Valley Life", "kind": "paragraph", "start": 31196, "end": 31227}, {"text": "RELATED TEXT: VALLEY “Everything is flowing,” John Muir has written, “going somewhere, animals and so-called lifeless rocks as well as water.” Most of the year, the Merced River flows peacefully through Yosemite Valley. Shrubs and deciduous trees enrich the riverbanks with green ribbons of life. Moist meadows give way to black oak trees that provide nutritious acorns to deer, bears, and woodpeckers, as they did for early American Indians. A flooding Merced River, however, seems to shout “change” and reconfigures nature’s handiwork.", "heading_path": "OVERVIEW: Front Side of Brochure > IMAGE and TEXT: Valley Life", "kind": "paragraph", "start": 31229, "end": 31766}, {"text": "Spend time in Yosemite Valley and you will experience change. Whether it’s the subtle daily changes in the flow of rivers and waterfalls, or the explosive makeover of a flood or 100-ton rockfall, nature undergoes constant transformation here. Water has played an important role in the geologic processes responsible for the stunning appearance of this “incomparable valley.”", "heading_path": "OVERVIEW: Front Side of Brochure > IMAGE and TEXT: Valley Life", "kind": "paragraph", "start": 31768, "end": 32142}, {"text": "Yosemite Valley, with the Mariposa Grove, inspired the national park idea. The cliffs, waterfalls, wildlife, and beauty of this place continue to inspire people around the world.", "heading_path": "OVERVIEW: Front Side of Brochure > IMAGE and TEXT: Valley Life", "kind": "paragraph", "start": 32144, "end": 32322}, {"text": "IMAGE: Ansel Adams", "heading_path": "OVERVIEW: Front Side of Brochure > IMAGE: Ansel Adams", "kind": "paragraph", "start": 32324, "end": 32342}, {"text": "DESCRIBING: A black and white photo of a middle-aged Ansel Adams, seated and smiling.", "heading_path": "OVERVIEW: Front Side of Brochure > IMAGE: Ansel Adams", "kind": "paragraph", "start": 32344, "end": 32429}, {"text": "SYNOPSIS: A black and white photo captioned, \"\"Yosemite Valley, to me, is always a sunrise, a glitter of green and golden wonder in a vast edifice of stone and space.\" Ansel Adams, photographer\" and credited to © Jim Alinder shows an elder Ansel Adams looking directly at the camera, sitting with an easy forward slouch. His left leg is crossed over his right knee and both aged arthritic hands are loosely grasping his crossed leg. He wears a multi-pocketed vest over a long-sleeved, plaid, button-down shirt, and creased slacks. His dark clothes contrast sharply with his white laced up shoes. He has a white short-haired beard and mustache, and a warm open-mouth smile that shows his top row of teeth, giving him pronounced cheeks. His head is somewhat tilted to his right and he is wearing a light-colored cowboy hat that emphasizes his ears, which slightly point outward at the top.", "heading_path": "OVERVIEW: Front Side of Brochure > IMAGE: Ansel Adams", "kind": "paragraph", "start": 32431, "end": 33318}, {"text": "CAPTION: \"Yosemite Valley, to me, is always a sunrise, a glitter of green and golden wonder in a vast edifice of stone and space.\" Ansel Adams, photographer.", "heading_path": "OVERVIEW: Front Side of Brochure > IMAGE: Ansel Adams", "kind": "paragraph", "start": 33320, "end": 33477}, {"text": "CREDIT: Copyright Jim Alinder", "heading_path": "OVERVIEW: Front Side of Brochure > IMAGE: Ansel Adams", "kind": "paragraph", "start": 33479, "end": 33508}, {"text": "IMAGE: Black Bear", "heading_path": "OVERVIEW: Front Side of Brochure > IMAGE: Black Bear", "kind": "paragraph", "start": 33510, "end": 33527}, {"text": "DESCRIBING: A cutout image of a front-facing black bear standing on a log.", "heading_path": "OVERVIEW: Front Side of Brochure > IMAGE: Black Bear", "kind": "paragraph", "start": 33529, "end": 33603}, {"text": "SYNOPSIS: The image, captioned \"Black bear\" ( Ursus americanus ) and credited to Benjamin R. Miller of Closerlook Photography, shows a front-facing bear that, in contradiction to its name, has reddish-brown fur. Only the front two legs are shown, with its cushioned paws slightly turned inward. The bear is standing on a grey textured log that shows off its claws which protrude out from its paws and curve down into sharp points. A full round face with a long yellow snout is capped off with a large, round, black nose. A small insert at the top right corner of the map shows the wilderness region. A small inset near the center of the map shows Yosemite Valley and says, \"See Valley Map Below.\" A series of text blocks beside the map discuss wilderness, rivers and waterfalls, wildlife, smoke and fire, as well as human history. A second, smaller map located off to the right and between the two major sections, shows Yosemite's location in relation to major highways, as well as Sequoia, Kings Canyon, and Death Valley National Parks.", "heading_path": "OVERVIEW: Back Side of Brochure", "kind": "paragraph", "start": 37453, "end": 38070}, {"text": "At the bottom of the page lies the section entitled \"Yosemite Basics.\" The above-mentioned inset is expanded to show details of Yosemite Valley. On the left of the Yosemite Valley map at the bottom of the page is a text portion regarding driving, reservations, accessibility and contact information.", "heading_path": "OVERVIEW: Back Side of Brochure", "kind": "paragraph", "start": 38072, "end": 38371}, {"text": "MAP and TEXT: Yosemite Park Map", "heading_path": "OVERVIEW: Back Side of Brochure > MAP and TEXT: Yosemite Park Map", "kind": "paragraph", "start": 38373, "end": 38404}, {"text": "DESCRIBING: Orientation map of Yosemite National Park", "heading_path": "OVERVIEW: Back Side of Brochure > MAP and TEXT: Yosemite Park Map", "kind": "paragraph", "start": 38406, "end": 38459}, {"text": "SYNOPSIS: This wayfinding and orientation map shows Yosemite National Park along with its major roads, points of interest, services, trails, and physical features.", "heading_path": "OVERVIEW: Back Side of Brochure > MAP and TEXT: Yosemite Park Map", "kind": "paragraph", "start": 38461, "end": 38624}, {"text": "IN-DEPTH DESCRIPTION: This orientation map shows all of Yosemite National Park and is oriented north at the top. It provides wayfinding information for points of interest, major roads and services, as well as the main trails and geographic information such as peaks and waterways. It is the largest of the four maps on the back side of this brochure.", "heading_path": "OVERVIEW: Back Side of Brochure > MAP and TEXT: Yosemite Park Map", "kind": "paragraph", "start": 38626, "end": 38976}, {"text": "The park is shown surrounded by national forest and wilderness lands in the heart of the Sierra Nevada mountain range of California. Roughly oval, like an egg standing on its small end, the park's irregular boundary primarily follows the alpine peaks on the northern and eastern edges with a more angular boundary line to the south and west. The park is roughly the size of the state of Rhode Island. Nearly all wilderness, the park is crisscrossed with hiking trails. There are two primary watersheds, the Tuolumne River to the north and the Merced River to the south. The two watersheds are roughly divided in upper and lower halves by 59-mile Tioga Road, which connects with Highway 120 east of Tioga Pass. The rest of the roads within the park either run along the western border, such as the Big Oak Flat Road and the Wawona Road or are spur roads that travel eastward no farther than halfway across the distance of the park. The spurs include Hetch Hetchy Road, El Portal Road to Yosemite Valley, Glacier Point Road, and the Mariposa Grove Road.", "heading_path": "OVERVIEW: Back Side of Brochure > MAP and TEXT: Yosemite Park Map", "kind": "paragraph", "start": 38978, "end": 40029}, {"text": "The park has three main administrative districts: Wawona in the south, Yosemite Valley in the central area of the park, and the Mather district covering the northern half of the park. Each district contains a visitor center or information station (two in Mather), one or two primary roads, visitor amenities, and an entrance station (three in Mather).", "heading_path": "OVERVIEW: Back Side of Brochure > MAP and TEXT: Yosemite Park Map", "kind": "paragraph", "start": 40031, "end": 40382}, {"text": "The park entrances, each near the park boundary, will be described with Yosemite as a clock face. The Tioga Pass entrance is at 2:30. It is in the Mather District near Tuolumne Meadows and lies along Tioga Road. 18 miles to the west is the Tuolumne Meadows Visitor Center. South Entrance is at 6:30. It is in the Wawona District and lies along Wawona Road (continuation of Highway 41 from outside the park. 7.5 miles to the north is the Wawona Visitor Center inside Hill's Studio. Arch Rock entrance is at 7:30. It is in the Valley District and lies along El Portal Road (continuation of Highway 140 from outside the park). 11.4 miles to the east is the Yosemite Valley Welcome Center.", "heading_path": "OVERVIEW: Back Side of Brochure > MAP and TEXT: Yosemite Park Map", "kind": "paragraph", "start": 40384, "end": 41069}, {"text": "Big Oak Flat entrance is at 8:30. It is in the Mather District and lies along Big Oak Flat Road (continuation of Highway 120 from west of Yosemite). At the entrance is the Big Oak Flat Information Station.", "heading_path": "OVERVIEW: Back Side of Brochure > MAP and TEXT: Yosemite Park Map", "kind": "paragraph", "start": 41071, "end": 41276}, {"text": "Hetch Hetchy entrance is at 9:30. It is also in the Mather District and lies along the Hetch Hetchy Road.", "heading_path": "OVERVIEW: Back Side of Brochure > MAP and TEXT: Yosemite Park Map", "kind": "paragraph", "start": 41278, "end": 41383}, {"text": "Special notices on the map include winter road closures from approximately November to May, including Tioga Road from the Tuolumne Grove parking lot on the west side to the Tioga Pass entrance on the east side. Glacier Point Road from the Badger Pass Ski Area east, and all of the Mariposa Grove Road. Facilities along the Tioga Road are available in summer only. Restrooms are available at picnic areas, campgrounds, trailheads, and roadside pullouts along the Tioga Road. Lastly, there is no swimming or boating in the Hetch Hetchy Reservoir.", "heading_path": "OVERVIEW: Back Side of Brochure > MAP and TEXT: Yosemite Park Map", "kind": "paragraph", "start": 41385, "end": 41929}, {"text": "This map does not include accessibility symbols.", "heading_path": "OVERVIEW: Back Side of Brochure > MAP and TEXT: Yosemite Park Map", "kind": "paragraph", "start": 41931, "end": 41979}, {"text": "MAP: YNP Legend", "heading_path": "OVERVIEW: Back Side of Brochure > MAP and TEXT: Yosemite Park Map > MAP: YNP Legend", "kind": "paragraph", "start": 41981, "end": 41996}, {"text": "A symbol shows north is up on the map. The major road, the El Portal Road, runs east from the entrance. Amenities are listed east to west along the road.", "heading_path": "OVERVIEW: Back Side of Brochure > MAP and TEXT: Yosemite Park Map > MAP: YNP Amenities > Valley District Amenities", "kind": "paragraph", "start": 46672, "end": 46844}, {"text": "El Portal area – food, picnic areas, gas (For other amenities see map below.)", "heading_path": "OVERVIEW: Back Side of Brochure > MAP and TEXT: Yosemite Park Map > MAP: YNP Amenities > Valley District Amenities", "kind": "paragraph", "start": 46846, "end": 46923}, {"text": "Cascade Creek – picnic area", "heading_path": "OVERVIEW: Back Side of Brochure > MAP and TEXT: Yosemite Park Map > MAP: YNP Amenities > Valley District Amenities", "kind": "paragraph", "start": 46925, "end": 46952}, {"text": "Yosemite Valley Welcome Center and Theater – wilderness permit station", "heading_path": "OVERVIEW: Back Side of Brochure > MAP and TEXT: Yosemite Park Map > MAP: YNP Amenities > Valley District Amenities", "kind": "paragraph", "start": 46954, "end": 47024}, {"text": "(See Yosemite Basics map for more amenities in Yosemite Valley.)", "heading_path": "OVERVIEW: Back Side of Brochure > MAP and TEXT: Yosemite Park Map > MAP: YNP Amenities > Valley District Amenities", "kind": "paragraph", "start": 47026, "end": 47090}, {"text": "MAP: YNP Roads", "heading_path": "OVERVIEW: Back Side of Brochure > MAP and TEXT: Yosemite Park Map > MAP: YNP Roads", "kind": "paragraph", "start": 47092, "end": 47106}, {"text": "Mather District Roads", "heading_path": "OVERVIEW: Back Side of Brochure > MAP and TEXT: Yosemite Park Map > MAP: YNP Roads > Mather District Roads", "kind": "paragraph", "start": 47108, "end": 47129}, {"text": "East of the park, Highway 395 runs north-south past Mono Lake and the small town of Lee Vining. Highway 120 climbs 13 miles out of Lee Vining, through the Inyo National Forest and up to Tioga Pass Entrance. It is at this point that the road closes to the west approximately November to May. From Tioga Pass, the road is named Tioga Road, and runs 59 miles east to west, bisecting the park into north and south sections. The road ends near the western boundary at the Big Oak Flat Road and Crane Flat Gas Station.", "heading_path": "OVERVIEW: Back Side of Brochure > MAP and TEXT: Yosemite Park Map > MAP: YNP Roads > Mather District Roads", "kind": "paragraph", "start": 47131, "end": 47643}, {"text": "From Highway 99 in Manteca, Highway 120 enters from the western side of the park. Just outside the park boundary, a 20-mile spur road, Evergreen Road, runs north to connect Highway 120 with Hetch Hetchy Road in the town of Mather. From here, the eight-mile Hetch Hetchy Road soon enters the park at the Hetch Hetchy Entrance and wilderness permit station. The road then runs northeast to the Hetch Hetchy Valley and Reservoir. A small loop road at the reservoir allows visitors to turn around. Vehicles are limited to 25 feet (8 meters) in length and 8 feet (2.4 meters) in width on this narrow winding road.", "heading_path": "OVERVIEW: Back Side of Brochure > MAP and TEXT: Yosemite Park Map > MAP: YNP Roads > Mather District Roads", "kind": "paragraph", "start": 47645, "end": 48253}, {"text": "From the start of the Evergreen Road on Highway 120, it is just over a mile to the south to arrive at the Big Oak Flat Entrance Station. Inside the park, the 17 miles of the continuation of Highway 120 that travels down to El Portal Road is known as Big Oak Flat Road. Nearly 8 miles to the southeast from Big Oak Flat Entrance is the Crane Flat Gas Station. The start of the Tioga Road is at this junction. From the gas station, the cliffside Big Oak Flat Road winds and drops 10 more miles, traveling through two tunnels to arrive at El Portal Road.", "heading_path": "OVERVIEW: Back Side of Brochure > MAP and TEXT: Yosemite Park Map > MAP: YNP Roads > Mather District Roads", "kind": "paragraph", "start": 48255, "end": 48806}, {"text": "Wawona District Roads", "heading_path": "OVERVIEW: Back Side of Brochure > MAP and TEXT: Yosemite Park Map > MAP: YNP Roads > Wawona District Roads", "kind": "paragraph", "start": 48808, "end": 48829}, {"text": "From Fresno, Highway 41 travels 61 miles north to Yosemite. Fish Camp lies just outside the park boundary. Just inside the park boundary is the South Entrance.", "heading_path": "OVERVIEW: Back Side of Brochure > MAP and TEXT: Yosemite Park Map > MAP: YNP Roads > Wawona District Roads", "kind": "paragraph", "start": 48831, "end": 48990}, {"text": "Parking is available there to take a bus east up a small spur road, Mariposa Grove Road. This road leads to the Mariposa Grove of Giant Sequoias, the park’s largest sequoia grove. This road is closed approximately December to April. Use mandatory shuttle approximately April to November. 25ft vehicle limit and no trailers allowed. The 31 miles of the continuation of Highway 41 into the park", "heading_path": "OVERVIEW: Back Side of Brochure > MAP and TEXT: Yosemite Park Map > MAP: YNP Roads > Wawona District Roads", "kind": "paragraph", "start": 48992, "end": 49384}, {"text": "to Yosemite Valley is called Wawona Road. Five miles north of the South Entrance is the town of Wawona with two small spur roads leading up to a collection of homes. 18 miles to the north of the South Entrance, a spur road on the left leads to a collection of homes just outside the park boundary known as Yosemite West. Less than a mile beyond and on the right is Chinquapin, the start of Glacier Point Road. Five miles up Glacier Point Road to the east lies the Badger Pass Ski Area. The road is closed approximately November to May east of Badger Pass Ski Area but may be open December to March to the ski area. This winding, mountain road heads east, then north for 16.5 miles to arrive at Glacier Point and the rim of Yosemite Valley. The Wawona Road ends at Southside Drive in Yosemite Valley, east of the end of El Portal Road.", "heading_path": "OVERVIEW: Back Side of Brochure > MAP and TEXT: Yosemite Park Map > MAP: YNP Roads > Wawona District Roads", "kind": "paragraph", "start": 49386, "end": 50220}, {"text": "Yosemite Valley District Roads", "heading_path": "OVERVIEW: Back Side of Brochure > MAP and TEXT: Yosemite Park Map > MAP: YNP Roads > Yosemite Valley District Roads", "kind": "paragraph", "start": 50222, "end": 50252}, {"text": "Starting in Merced, the 65-mile Highway 140 travels from the southwest up to El Portal. Across the river to the north, a small road leaves from El Portal, parallels the river and runs west for about 4 miles. From El Portal to Yosemite Valley, Highway 140 is called El Portal Road. 3.7 miles to the west of El Portal is the Arch Rock Entrance. 5 miles beyond to the east, the southern terminus of the Big Oak Flat Road joins El Portal Road. 2 miles to the east beyond the Big Oak Flat junction lies the northern terminus of Wawona Road. El Portal Road ends in Yosemite Valley; the primary roads of which are Northside and Southside Drives which run in a loop around the edge of the seven mile long valley. See Valley Map for more details.", "heading_path": "OVERVIEW: Back Side of Brochure > MAP and TEXT: Yosemite Park Map > MAP: YNP Roads > Yosemite Valley District Roads", "kind": "paragraph", "start": 50254, "end": 50991}, {"text": "MAP: YNP Trails", "heading_path": "OVERVIEW: Back Side of Brochure > MAP and TEXT: Yosemite Park Map > MAP: YNP Trails", "kind": "paragraph", "start": 50993, "end": 51008}, {"text": "Extensive hiking trails indicated by dashed grey and olive-green lines cover the Yosemite landscape in over 700 miles of trails. A selection of renowned trails will be highlighted here. When relevant, the park boundary will be referenced as a clock face with north at twelve o'clock.", "heading_path": "OVERVIEW: Back Side of Brochure > MAP and TEXT: Yosemite Park Map > MAP: YNP Trails", "kind": "paragraph", "start": 51010, "end": 51293}, {"text": "The Pacific Crest Trail enters the park boundary from the north in the Yosemite Wilderness and travels down to cross the Tioga Road at Tuolumne Meadows. From there, it passes through Tuolumne Meadows, southeast down Lyell Canyon and out of the park's southern wilderness area and out the eastern boundary. From Yosemite Valley, the famous John Muir Trail starts up the Mist Trail traveling northeast, passing by the west end of Little Yosemite Valley, crossing through Tuolumne Meadows and joining the Pacific Crest Trail. The John Muir Trail ends 210 miles later at Mount Whitney in Sequoia National Park. Starting from the Mist Trail at the north of Little Yosemite Valley, a spur trail branches north to access Half Dome. Further trails leaving from Yosemite Valley can be found in the Trails section of the map entitled Services and Facilities of Yosemite Valley.", "heading_path": "OVERVIEW: Back Side of Brochure > MAP and TEXT: Yosemite Park Map > MAP: YNP Trails", "kind": "paragraph", "start": 51295, "end": 52162}, {"text": "All three groves of giant sequoias have hiking trails. In the Wawona District off of the Mariposa Grove Road, a 5- to 6-mile loop trail takes visitors through the upper and lower groves. In the Mather District off the Big Oak Flat Road northeast of Crane Flat, a 1.5-mile trail drops from the Merced Grove Parking Area down to the Merced Grove. Just north of Crane Flat on Tioga Road lies a restroom and parking area for Tuolumne Grove. A 1.5-mile trail leads down to the grove. From the Lembert Dome Parking Area in Tuolumne Meadows along the Tioga Road, a 1.5 mile round trip hike takes you to Soda Springs and Parsons Lodge.", "heading_path": "OVERVIEW: Back Side of Brochure > MAP and TEXT: Yosemite Park Map > MAP: YNP Trails", "kind": "paragraph", "start": 52164, "end": 52791}, {"text": "More detailed day-hiking maps of each district are available at all visitor centers and wilderness permit stations. Finely detailed topographic maps of discrete regions are available at all Yosemite wilderness permit stations. For specific requests of more detailed descriptions of any Yosemite park map, please call the Yosemite Accessibility Line at [phone redacted].", "heading_path": "OVERVIEW: Back Side of Brochure > MAP and TEXT: Yosemite Park Map > MAP: YNP Trails", "kind": "paragraph", "start": 52793, "end": 53162}, {"text": "MAP: YNP Highlights", "heading_path": "OVERVIEW: Back Side of Brochure > MAP and TEXT: Yosemite Park Map > MAP: YNP Highlights", "kind": "paragraph", "start": 53164, "end": 53183}, {"text": "Surrounding the park’s boundary are a series of national forests and wilderness areas which are as follows. To the west, northwest and due north are the Stanislaus National Forest and Emigrant Wilderness. To the northeast lies the Humboldt-Toiyabe National Forest and Hoover Wilderness. To the east is the Inyo National Forest. To the southeast is the Ansel Adams Wilderness. Lastly, to the south and southwest lies the Stanislaus National Forest. Yosemite National Park is an extremely large area with countless frontcountry and backcountry highlights including meadows, domes, peaks, waterfalls, trees, viewpoints and trails, as well as historic features such as buildings and bridges. "MAP: YNP Topography", "heading_path": "OVERVIEW: Back Side of Brochure > MAP and TEXT: Yosemite Park Map > MAP: YNP Topography", "kind": "paragraph", "start": 55726, "end": 55745}, {"text": "Located on the western slope of the Sierra Nevada, the park has a wide elevation range. Starting from about 2,000 feet in the foothill community of El Portal at the western edge, the area is rocky and dry with grasses, shrubs and oak woodlands. That landscape transitions to rocky, dry shrub land with few trees. At higher elevations, such as Yosemite Valley, is a diversity of tree species with oaks, pines, cedars and firs. Giant Sequoias grow in contained areas at four to six thousand feet. Further up the mountains, the trees shift to primarily firs and pines, and near 8,000 feet, the trees are a mix of pines and hemlocks, contorted and stunted from the deep snow in winter. Beyond the treeline, the landscape rises to a dramatic crest of snowy, treeless peaks along the eastern side of over 13,000 feet. Interestingly, from the eastern Tioga Pass of 9,945 feet at the park line, the landscape drops dramatically in just five miles to the east, down to the shore of Mono Lake at 6,837 feet.", "heading_path": "OVERVIEW: Back Side of Brochure > MAP and TEXT: Yosemite Park Map > MAP: YNP Topography", "kind": "paragraph", "start": 55747, "end": 56744}, {"text": "The park's wilderness lands include rugged, mountainous terrain shown with shadowing on the map and two major watersheds with creeks and lakes shown in blue. North of Tioga Road lies the Tuolumne River drainage. The Tuolumne River runs roughly east to west, fed by countless tributary creeks and lakes across the jagged, dramatic landscape of pines and exposed granite. The river runs through many meadows, the largest of which is Tuolumne Meadows. A primary feature of the Tuolumne River is the extensive Grand Canyon of the Tuolumne which travels through Pate Valley before spilling into the Hetch Hetchy Reservoir on the west side of the park. The Hetch Hetchy Valley's 3,000-foot cliff walls stand testament to the park's glacial history.", "heading_path": "OVERVIEW: Back Side of Brochure > MAP and TEXT: Yosemite Park Map > MAP: YNP Topography", "kind": "paragraph", "start": 56746, "end": 57488}, {"text": "At the geographic center of the park lies Mount Hoffmann, at 10,850 feet. South of Tioga Road lies the Merced River drainage. The Merced River runs roughly east to west, as well. Like the Tuolumne River, the Merced is fed by tributary creeks and lakes across the rough, wilderness terrain. The Merced River includes Yosemite Valley, a flat bottomed, glacially carved valley with exposed 3,000-foot cliff walls.", "heading_path": "OVERVIEW: Back Side of Brochure > MAP and TEXT: Yosemite Park Map > MAP: YNP Topography", "kind": "paragraph", "start": 57490, "end": 57900}, {"text": "MAP: YNP Text by Quadrant Overview", "heading_path": "OVERVIEW: Back Side of Brochure > MAP: YNP Text by Quadrant Overview", "kind": "paragraph", "start": 57902, "end": 57936}, {"text": "This section covers all of the text and icons on the map.
